mainEntity.name: How much does a Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rebuilt Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi (D4FB/D4FD) engine typically costs between £1,500 and £3,200 for supply only, while reconditioned units start from £1,200.

mainEntity.name: What are the common signs of D4FB/D4FD engine failure in a Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi?

acceptedAnswer.text: Owners often report a metallic rattling noise on cold starts (timing chain), sudden loss of power, or frequent DPF warning lights.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the body, chassis, and interior are in good condition.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi engine replacement take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A standard supply and fit service for the Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi typically takes 2 to 3 days.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the D4FB and D4FD engine codes in the i30 1.6 CRDi?

acceptedAnswer.text: The D4FB is the earlier U2 diesel engine fitted to the first and second-generation i30 (2007-2017), while the D4FD is the updated version fitted to the third-generation (2017-present) with revised EGR and emissions calibration.

historyTimeline.h2: Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: When the 1.6 CRDi variant was introduced to the Hyundai i30 lineup, it brought the efficient and torque-rich U2 diesel engine to the compact family car segment, quickly becoming the best-selling diesel choice across the UK due to its balance of fuel economy and reliability.

milestones.description: D4FB (1.6L CRDi), 115hp, introduced with the first-generation (FD) i30, featuring common-rail direct injection and a variable geometry turbocharger.
D4FB (1.6L CRDi), 110hp / 128hp / 136hp, continued into the second-generation (GD) i30 with improved emissions controls, a 6-speed manual gearbox, and optional automatic transmission.
D4FD (1.6L CRDi), 115hp / 136hp, introduced in the third-generation (PD) i30, featuring updated EGR and DPF systems for stricter Euro 6 compliance and refined NVH levels.

historyTimeline.closingNote: Every engine fitted to the Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi is covered below, with UK rebuilt pricing and known failure points.

commonProblems.h2: Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi (D4FB/D4FD) is generally a robust and economical diesel, but like all modern diesels, it is susceptible to specific wear points related to emissions systems and timing components. Rebuilt engines sourced through EnginesMarket include upgraded internal components designed to address these original failure points, backed by a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: Timing Chain Tensioner Failure - Why the Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi D4FB Suffers Rattling
problems.rootCause: The hydraulic timing chain tensioner gradually loses pressure due to oil flow restrictions or extended service intervals, allowing chain slack. This causes a distinct rattling noise on cold starts and can eventually lead to skipped teeth and catastrophic valve damage.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Engine-out service to replace timing chain, tensioners, guides, and oil pump drive.
repairOptions.longevity: Viable only if caught before valve contact. Extends life 60k+ miles.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete swapped unit with upgraded tensioner design, bench-tested compression, and full supply & fit.
repairOptions.longevity: Permanent solution. Restores factory torque and reliability with 12-month warranty.

problems.recommendation: We strongly advise against intermediate repairs once timing chain jump has occurred. On a Hyundai i30 valued at £1,500-£6,000 depending on generation, the labour intensity and hidden block damage make a full rebuilt engine swap the only reliable and cost-effective choice.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt D4FB engine prices for your Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi

problems.h4: EGR Cooler Leaks & DPF Blockage - Why the Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi Loses Power
problems.rootCause: Factory-supplied EGR cooler housings can develop micro-fractures from thermal cycling, allowing coolant to seep into the intake. Concurrently, short urban journeys prevent DPF regeneration, leading to progressive soot buildup, back-pressure, and eventual engine management warnings.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Drain cooling system, fit updated EGR cooler assembly, flush intake, and reflash ECU for DPF sync.
repairOptions.longevity: Highly effective if caught early before cylinder hydro-lock occurs.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete replacement unit with updated EGR/DPF calibration, fresh turbo seals, and full supply & fit.
repairOptions.longevity: Essential if coolant has already caused bearing wash-out or hydro-lock.

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2007-2023 Hyundai i30 1.6 CRDi holds a market value of approximately £1,500-£8,000 depending on year, generation, and condition [THIRD-PARTY]. Because this falls into the £1,500-£8,000 band, a reconditioned or rebuilt engine is highly justified if the chassis, body, and interior are in good condition, as the replacement cost represents a sensible fraction of the vehicle's overall worth.
problems.recommendation: If your i30 1.6 CRDi still runs cleanly and has not ingested coolant, the minor preventative replacement is the smartest financial move. However, if white smoke, coolant loss, or misfires are already present, we recommend skipping partial repairs and moving straight to a rebuilt engine to avoid catastrophic secondary damage.
